Functorial Neural Architectures from Higher Inductive Types

Karen Sargsyan Email: karen.sarkisyan@gmail.com Affiliation: Institute of Chemistry, Academia Sinica, Taipei, Taiwan
Abstract

Neural networks systematically fail at compositional generalization—producing correct outputs for novel combinations of known parts. We show that this failure is architectural: compositional generalization is equivalent to functoriality of the decoder, and this perspective yields both guarantees and impossibility results. We compile Higher Inductive Type (HIT) specifications into neural architectures via a monoidal functor from the path groupoid of a target space to a category of parametric maps: path constructors become generator networks, composition becomes structural concatenation, and 2-cells witnessing group relations become learned natural transformations. We prove that decoders assembled by structural concatenation of independently generated segments are strict monoidal functors (compositional by construction), while softmax self-attention is not functorial for any non-trivial compositional task. Both results are formalized in Cubical Agda. Experiments on three spaces validate the full hierarchy: on the torus (ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}), functorial decoders outperform non-functorial ones by 22–2.7×2.7\times; on S1∨S1S^{1}\vee S^{1} (F2F_{2}), the type-A/B gap widens to 5.55.5–10×10\times; on the Klein bottle (ℤ⋊ℤ\mathbb{Z}\rtimes\mathbb{Z}), a learned 2-cell closes a 46%46\% error gap on words exercising the group relation.

1 Introduction

A model that has learned to add 2-digit numbers should handle 5-digit numbers—the algorithm is the same, applied to more parts. A robot that can navigate around one obstacle should handle two obstacles by composing single-obstacle plans. A language model trained on simple commands should handle “go left then right” without retraining. In each case, the task decomposes into parts that combine by a known rule, and the model must respect that rule on inputs never seen during training. This is compositional generalization, and neural networks systematically fail at it. Standard neural networks fail on SCAN [1] (linguistic composition), COGS [2] (semantic parsing), and multi-step arithmetic [3]. These failures are not capacity limitations—they persist as models scale.

We argue that the failure is architectural. Consider a decoder that handles a combined input by producing each part’s output independently, then combining the results: 𝒟⁡(w1⋅w2)=𝒟⁡(w1)⊕𝒟⁡(w2)\mathcal{D}(w_{1}\cdot w_{2})=\mathcal{D}(w_{1})\oplus\mathcal{D}(w_{2}). In categorical language, this equation says the decoder is a monoidal functor from the input algebra to the output algebra. We prove that a specific class of decoders (transport decoders) are monoidal functors (Theorem 3.3), and that softmax attention is not one, for any choice of parameters (Theorem 4.1). The reason is concrete: two different input sequences can represent the same compositional meaning (e.g., a​bab and b​aba in an abelian group), so a compositional decoder must produce the same output for both. But attention computes different key vectors for different token orderings, producing different outputs regardless of the learned weights.

The principle that compositional semantics is functoriality originates in DisCoCat [4, 5]. To realize this principle in learnable systems, one needs a categorical account of neural architectures themselves; categorical deep learning [6, 7, 8] provides this, organizing parametric maps into categories and formalizing learning and architectural constraints via functorial and algebraic structure. But in both programmes, building a functorial architecture for a given compositional structure—say ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} for the torus, F2F_{2} for two-obstacle navigation—requires ad hoc engineering with no guarantee that the result is actually functorial. We provide the missing step: a compilation functor from Higher Inductive Type (HIT) specifications to neural architectures, so that the algebraic structure of the task determines the architecture automatically, with compositional correctness by construction. Experiments show that the resulting architectures outperform non-functorial alternatives by 22–10×10\times.

Contributions.

(1) A compilation functor mapping HIT constructors—basepoints, loops, 2-cells—to architectural components—generator networks, structural concatenation, learned homotopies—so that compositional correctness is guaranteed by construction (§3). (2) Transport decoders (which concatenate independently generated segments) are strict monoidal functors; softmax attention is not, for any parameters. Both results are formalized in Cubical Agda (§4). (3) Experiments on T2T^{2} (fundamental group π1=ℤ2\pi_{1}=\mathbb{Z}^{2}, abelian), S1∨S1S^{1}\vee S^{1} (π1=F2\pi_{1}=F_{2}, free), and Klein bottle (π1=ℤ⋊ℤ\pi_{1}=\mathbb{Z}\rtimes\mathbb{Z}, semidirect product) validate all three levels: winding constraints, monoidal composition, and a learned 2-cell witnessing a group relation (§5).

2 From Types to Categories

The three ingredients below—HIT specifications, monoidal structure of π1\pi_{1}, and parametric maps—combine in §3 to give the compilation functor. The reader familiar with HoTT and categorical deep learning may skip to §3.

2.1 Spaces from generators and relations

To build decoders with topological guarantees, we need a specification language that describes spaces by their generators and relations—much as a group presentation describes a group by generators and relations. Higher inductive types provide exactly this.

In HoTT [9, 10], every type AA has an identity type a=Aba=_{A}b. Elements p:a=bp:a=b are paths; they compose (p⋅q:a=cp\cdot q:a=c), have inverses (p−1:b=ap^{-1}:b=a), and satisfy groupoid laws up to higher coherence. The loop space Ω⁡(A,a):=(a=a)\Omega(A,a):=(a=a) carries a group structure up to higher coherence under path composition; its set-truncation ‖Ω⁡(A,a)‖0\|{\Omega(A,a)}\|_{0} is the group π1​(A,a)\pi_{1}(A,a).

A Higher Inductive Type (HIT) specifies a type by listing its constructors at each dimension: a basepoint, loops (paths from the basepoint to itself), and 2-cells (homotopies between loops witnessing algebraic relations). Three examples drive the paper:

Torus T2T^{2}: base:T2\textsf{base}:T^{2}; loopa,loopb:base=base\mathrm{loop}_{a},\mathrm{loop}_{b}:\textsf{base}=\textsf{base}; surf:loopa⋅loopb=loopb⋅loopa\textsf{surf}:\mathrm{loop}_{a}\cdot\mathrm{loop}_{b}=\mathrm{loop}_{b}\cdot\mathrm{loop}_{a}.
π1​(T2)=ℤ2\pi_{1}(T^{2})=\mathbb{Z}^{2} (abelian; the 2-cell surf witnesses commutativity).

Wedge of circles S1∨S1S^{1}\vee S^{1}: base; loopa,loopb:base=base\mathrm{loop}_{a},\mathrm{loop}_{b}:\textsf{base}=\textsf{base}; no 2-cells.
π1​(S1∨S1)=F2\pi_{1}(S^{1}\vee S^{1})=F_{2} (free group; no relations, a​b≠b​aab\neq ba).

Klein bottle KK: base; loopa,loopb\mathrm{loop}_{a},\mathrm{loop}_{b}; rel:loopb⋅loopa⋅loopb−1=loopa−1\textsf{rel}:\mathrm{loop}_{b}\cdot\mathrm{loop}_{a}\cdot\mathrm{loop}_{b}^{-1}=\mathrm{loop}_{a}^{-1}.
π1(K)=⟨a,b∣bab−1=a−1⟩≅ℤ⋊ℤ\pi_{1}(K)=\langle a,b\mid bab^{-1}=a^{-1}\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}\rtimes\mathbb{Z} (non-trivial relation).

These three span a hierarchy: abelian with a 2-cell (T2T^{2}), non-abelian without one (S1∨S1S^{1}\vee S^{1}), and non-abelian with a non-trivial 2-cell (KK). Each exercises a different level of the compilation functor in §3.

2.2 Composition as monoidal structure

The word “compositional” needs a precise meaning. We need a category whose monoidal product is word concatenation, so that a decoder preserving this product is compositional by definition—not by empirical evaluation on a test set.

A group G=⟨a1,…,ak∣r1,…,rm⟩G=\langle a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}\mid r_{1},\ldots,r_{m}\rangle can be viewed as a single-object category B​GBG: the morphisms are elements of GG, and composition is the group operation—i.e., word concatenation followed by reduction via the relations rjr_{j}. This category is monoidal under composition. When G=π1​(X,x0)G=\pi_{1}(X,x_{0}), the morphisms are homotopy classes of loops and composition is path concatenation.

A decoder is then a functor 𝒟:B​G→𝒞\mathcal{D}:BG\to\mathcal{C} into some target category. If 𝒟\mathcal{D} preserves the monoidal product—𝒟⁡(w1⋅w2)=𝒟⁡(w1)⊕𝒟⁡(w2)\mathcal{D}(w_{1}\cdot w_{2})=\mathcal{D}(w_{1})\oplus\mathcal{D}(w_{2})—it is a monoidal functor, and compositional by construction.

2.3 Neural networks as parametric maps

To land the compilation functor, we need a target category whose morphisms are neural networks. Following Cruttwell et al. [6] and Gavranović et al. [7], a neural network layer is a parametric map (Θ,f:Θ×X→Y)(\Theta,\,f:\Theta\times X\to Y)—a morphism in the category 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐚⁡(𝐒𝐦𝐨𝐨𝐭𝐡)\mathbf{Para}(\mathbf{Smooth}) parameterized by weights θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta. Composing two layers pairs their parameter spaces: (Θ1×Θ2,g∘f)(\Theta_{1}\times\Theta_{2},\;g\circ f). Fong, Spivak, and Tuyéras [8] show that gradient descent defines a monoidal functor from 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐚\mathbf{Para} to a category of learners, so anything landing in 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐚\mathbf{Para} is trainable by backpropagation.

Our compilation functor targets a subcategory: it maps each generator of π1​(X)\pi_{1}(X) to a parametric loop in 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐚⁡(𝐒𝐦𝐨𝐨𝐭𝐡)\mathbf{Para}(\mathbf{Smooth}), and composition in π1\pi_{1} maps to concatenation of loop segments. Functoriality of this map is compositional generalization. The next section makes this concrete.

3 From Specifications to Architectures

Let XX be a pointed connected space with π1(X)=G=⟨a1,…,ak∣r1,…,rm⟩\pi_{1}(X)=G=\langle a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}\mid r_{1},\ldots,r_{m}\rangle.

Definition 3.1 (Parametric loops).

𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐩⁡(X)\mathbf{ParLoop}(X) is the monoidal category with a single object ⋆\star (the basepoint x0x_{0}), whose morphisms ⋆→⋆\star\to\star are parametric loops (Θ,L:Θ×[0,1]→X)(\Theta,\,L:\Theta\times[0,1]\to X) with L⁡(θ,0)=L⁡(θ,1)=x0L(\theta,0)=L(\theta,1)=x_{0} for all θ\theta, and whose monoidal product is loop concatenation: (L1⊕L2)​(t)=L1​(2​t)(L_{1}\oplus L_{2})(t)=L_{1}(2t) for t≤12t\leq\tfrac{1}{2}, L2​(2​t−1)L_{2}(2t{-}1) for t>12t>\tfrac{1}{2}.

Construction 3.2 (HIT compilation).

Given a HIT for XX with π1​(X)=G\pi_{1}(X)=G, the compilation functor 𝒟:B​G→𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐩⁡(X)\mathcal{D}:BG\to\mathbf{ParLoop}(X) is:

  1. (i)

    Generators. For each generator aia_{i} of GG, a neural network gai​(θi,t):[0,1]→Xg_{a_{i}}(\theta_{i},t):[0,1]\to X (an MLP taking time tt and outputting a point on XX) producing a parametric loop whose winding number is constrained to [ai]∈π1​(X)[a_{i}]\in\pi_{1}(X) by construction. For inverses: gai−1​(θi,t):=gai​(θi,1−t)g_{a_{i}^{-1}}(\theta_{i},t):=g_{a_{i}}(\theta_{i},1-t).

  2. (ii)

    Composition. For a word w=ai1⋯aiLw=a_{i_{1}}\cdots a_{i_{L}}, 𝒟⁡(w):=gai1⊕⋯⊕gaiL\mathcal{D}(w):=g_{a_{i_{1}}}\oplus\cdots\oplus g_{a_{i_{L}}} (structural concatenation of the LL loop segments).

  3. (iii)

    2-cells. For each relation rj:LHSj=RHSjr_{j}:\text{LHS}_{j}=\text{RHS}_{j}, a parametric homotopy Hj:ΘjH×[0,1]s×[0,1]t→XH_{j}:\Theta_{j}^{H}\times[0,1]_{s}\times[0,1]_{t}\to X with boundary conditions Hj​(−,0,−)=𝒟⁡(LHSj)H_{j}(-,0,-)=\mathcal{D}(\text{LHS}_{j}), Hj​(−,1,−)=𝒟⁡(RHSj)H_{j}(-,1,-)=\mathcal{D}(\text{RHS}_{j})—a continuous deformation from one loop to the other, implemented as a separate MLP.

Theorem 3.3 (Transport composition = strict functoriality).

Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} be the transport decoder from Construction 3.2(i–ii).

  1. (a)

    Free monoid. For all words w1,w2w_{1},w_{2} over the generators and for all parameter values θ\theta:

    𝒟⁡(w1⋅w2)=𝒟⁡(w1)⊕𝒟⁡(w2).\mathcal{D}(w_{1}\cdot w_{2})\;=\;\mathcal{D}(w_{1})\oplus\mathcal{D}(w_{2}).

    That is, 𝒟\mathcal{D} is a strict monoidal functor from the free monoid on the generators to 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐩⁡(X)\mathbf{ParLoop}(X). This is an architectural identity, not a learned approximation.

  2. (b)

    Extension to GG. With the 2-cells of Construction 3.2(iii), 𝒟\mathcal{D} respects the group relations up to homotopy: for each relation rj:LHSj=RHSjr_{j}:\mathrm{LHS}_{j}=\mathrm{RHS}_{j}, the learned homotopy HjH_{j} provides a path 𝒟⁡(LHSj)≃𝒟⁡(RHSj)\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{LHS}_{j})\simeq\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{RHS}_{j}) in the loop space of XX. The result is a functor from B​GBG to the homotopy category of parametric loops: strict on composition, with HjH_{j} witnessing each relation.

Proof.

Part (a). Write w1=ai1⋯ainw_{1}=a_{i_{1}}\cdots a_{i_{n}} and w2=aj1⋯ajmw_{2}=a_{j_{1}}\cdots a_{j_{m}}. By Construction 3.2(ii):

𝒟⁡(w1⋅w2)=gai1⊕⋯⊕gain⊕gaj1⊕⋯⊕gajm=𝒟⁡(w1)⊕𝒟⁡(w2),\mathcal{D}(w_{1}\cdot w_{2})=g_{a_{i_{1}}}\oplus\cdots\oplus g_{a_{i_{n}}}\oplus g_{a_{j_{1}}}\oplus\cdots\oplus g_{a_{j_{m}}}=\mathcal{D}(w_{1})\oplus\mathcal{D}(w_{2}),

using associativity of ⊕\oplus. The unit law 𝒟⁡(e)=x0\mathcal{D}(e)=x_{0} holds by convention (the empty concatenation is the constant loop at x0x_{0}).

Part (b). Each HjH_{j} is a parametric homotopy satisfying the boundary conditions of Construction 3.2(iii). By definition, this makes 𝒟⁡(LHSj)\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{LHS}_{j}) and 𝒟⁡(RHSj)\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{RHS}_{j}) equal in the set-truncation ‖Ω⁡(X,x0)‖0=π1​(X)\|\Omega(X,x_{0})\|_{0}=\pi_{1}(X), so 𝒟\mathcal{D} descends to a well-defined map on the quotient B​GBG.

Formalized in Cubical Agda (TransportCoherence.agda). ∎

Remark 3.4 (Strict vs. up-to-reparametrization).

The continuous concatenation formula of Definition 3.1 (run L1L_{1} at double speed, then L2L_{2}) is associative only up to reparametrization of [0,1][0,1]. In the implementation, ⊕\oplus is point-cloud list-append, which is strictly associative. The strict functoriality of Theorem 3.3(a) relies on this discrete representation. In the continuous setting, the same result holds as a monoidal functor up to coherent reparametrization isomorphisms—a standard situation in homotopy theory, where path concatenation is associative only up to higher coherence.

Put simply: the transport decoder composes by list-append, and list-append is associative with an empty list as unit. No learning is involved in the composition step—it is a structural identity that holds for every parameter value and every word length.

Remark 3.5 (When the 2-cell matters).

On T2T^{2} and S1∨S1S^{1}\vee S^{1}, the 2-cell HH is either trivially satisfiable (abelian: any ordering is homotopic) or absent (free: no relations to witness). On KK, the relation b​a​b−1=a−1bab^{-1}=a^{-1} is non-trivial: after composing gb⊕ga⊕gb−1g_{b}\oplus g_{a}\oplus g_{b^{-1}}, the result must be homotopic to ga−1g_{a^{-1}}. Without HH, the transport decoder generates geometrically correct segments but globally incoherent loops—it ignores the frame flip. With HH, the decoder learns the deformation.

The topological constraints do not destroy geometric expressivity. Each generator gai​(θi)g_{a_{i}}(\theta_{i}) can represent any continuous loop in its homotopy class (by the universal approximation theorem for MLPs); the constraint acts only between classes, enforcing that 𝒟⁡(w)\mathcal{D}(w) is assembled from these generators. An alternative architecture—the cover decoder—assigns an independent shape to each homotopy class, giving strictly more geometric freedom. But this extra freedom is precisely the freedom to be incoherent: to produce outputs that violate composition. Functoriality trades inter-class freedom for the guarantee (Appendix J). This motivates a formal distinction:

Definition 3.6 (Type-A / Type-B).

An architecture is type-B (functorial) if its decoder defines a monoidal functor G→𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐩⁡(X)G\to\mathbf{ParLoop}(X) for all parameter values. It is type-A (non-functorial) otherwise.

Type-B architectures generate each loop segment independently from the corresponding generator network, then concatenate. Type-A architectures use cross-segment dependencies (e.g., attention between positions belonging to different generators), breaking the monoidal factorization 𝒟⁡(w1⋅w2)=𝒟⁡(w1)⊕𝒟⁡(w2)\mathcal{D}(w_{1}\cdot w_{2})=\mathcal{D}(w_{1})\oplus\mathcal{D}(w_{2}).

4 What Attention Cannot Compose

Construction 3.2 produces type-B architectures. We now show that the dominant composition mechanism in modern architectures—softmax attention—is inherently type-A: no parameter setting makes it functorial.

Softmax self-attention [11] aggregates information across positions via content-dependent weights: each position attends to every other position based on learned similarity between their representations, so every position’s output depends on the tokens at all other positions. (The standard formulation in terms of query, key, and value matrices is recalled in Appendix A.)

Theorem 4.1 (Attention is not functorial).

Let TθT_{\theta} be a transformer with softmax self-attention, and let GG be a non-trivial group. There exist no parameters θ\theta for which TθT_{\theta} defines a monoidal functor G→𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐩⁡(X)G\to\mathbf{ParLoop}(X).

Proof sketch (full proof in Appendix A).

Suppose for contradiction that TT is functorial, so T⁡(w1⋅w2)=T⁡(w1)⊕T⁡(w2)T(w_{1}\cdot w_{2})=T(w_{1})\oplus T(w_{2}). Since ⊕\oplus is a function of T⁡(w1)T(w_{1}) and T⁡(w2)T(w_{2}) alone, the output for the w1w_{1}-segment can depend on w2w_{2} only through T⁡(w2)T(w_{2}): any two words representing the same group element must produce the same effect on w1w_{1}’s output. But attention violates this: at each layer, position i∈w1i\in w_{1} attends to positions j∈w2j\in w_{2} via key vectors K​hjKh_{j} determined by the token embeddings of w2w_{2}, not by T⁡(w2)T(w_{2}). Since GG is non-trivial, there exist distinct words w2≠w2′w_{2}\neq w_{2}^{\prime} with [w2]=[w2′]∈G[w_{2}]=[w_{2}^{\prime}]\in G—same group element, different token sequences. Under any standard embedding (which maps distinct generator symbols to distinct vectors), these produce different key vectors, causing w1w_{1}’s output to differ between T⁡(w1⋅w2)T(w_{1}\cdot w_{2}) and T⁡(w1⋅w2′)T(w_{1}\cdot w_{2}^{\prime}), contradicting T⁡(w2)=T⁡(w2′)T(w_{2})=T(w_{2}^{\prime}). ∎

In short: attention is a content-based routing mechanism, and content-based routing cannot be compositional. A functorial decoder must treat all words representing the same group element identically, but attention reads the tokens themselves—not their equivalence class—so it distinguishes words that the functor must identify.

Scaling prediction.

For type-B decoders, the per-segment error is O⁡(1)O(1) as word length grows: each segment is generated independently by the same network. For type-A decoders, per-segment error degrades beyond the training word length because attention patterns over longer sequences are out-of-distribution (proved formally in Appendix I). The experiments in §5 confirm this across all three spaces.

Depth obstruction for nonsolvable groups.

The functoriality obstruction (Theorem 4.1) applies to all non-trivial groups, abelian or not. For groups with nonsolvable finite quotients (such as F2↠S5F_{2}\twoheadrightarrow S_{5}), a separate depth obstruction compounds the problem: prefix products are 𝖭𝖢1\mathsf{NC}^{1}-complete [12], outside the 𝖠𝖢0\mathsf{AC}^{0} circuit class that fixed-depth transformers implement. For solvable groups (such as ℤ⋊ℤ\mathbb{Z}\rtimes\mathbb{Z}), constant-depth shortcuts exist [21] and only the functoriality obstruction applies. The full trichotomy—abelian, solvable non-abelian, nonsolvable—is developed in Appendix H (Corollary H.2). Section 5.2 (F2F_{2}) tests both obstructions simultaneously; Section 5.3 (ℤ⋊ℤ\mathbb{Z}\rtimes\mathbb{Z}, solvable) isolates functoriality alone.

Relationship to DisCoCat and categorical deep learning.

Theorem 4.1 provides a structural impossibility result absent from prior work on functorial semantics: softmax cross-attention is incompatible with monoidal functoriality, whether the codomain is 𝐅𝐝𝐕𝐞𝐜𝐭\mathbf{FdVect} (as in DisCoCat [4, 5]) or 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐩⁡(X)\mathbf{ParLoop}(X). A stronger version (Appendix F) drops group structure entirely, requiring only sequential compositionality. The categorical deep learning programme [6, 8, 7] provides the semantic foundations we build on (§2); our contribution extends it from analysis to synthesis, deriving functorial architectures from type-theoretic specifications rather than analyzing existing ones.

5 Three Spaces, Three Predictions

The theorems make testable predictions: type-B decoders should show constant per-segment error as word length LL grows (Theorem 3.3), while type-A decoders should degrade (Theorem 4.1). We test on three spaces spanning the HIT hierarchy.

Task.

The task is continuous geometric generation: given a word w=w1⋯wLw=w_{1}\cdots w_{L} over generators of π1​(X)\pi_{1}(X), produce a point cloud γ^⊂ℝd\hat{\gamma}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} approximating a loop on XX in the homotopy class [w][w]—a curve that winds around XX in the way prescribed by ww (with d=3d=3 for T2T^{2} and S1∨S1S^{1}\vee S^{1}; d=4d=4 for KK). Training uses all words of length ≤2\leq 2 (6 words for T2T^{2} and S1∨S1S^{1}\vee S^{1}; 16 words for KK which has inverses); test words have length 3,4,6,8,103,4,6,8,10—never seen during training. This is up to a 5×5\times length extrapolation test. Ground-truth loops and data generation details are in Appendix B.

Architectures.

Table 1 summarizes the six decoders tested, classified by which HIT constructors they compile and whether they are functorial (type-B) or not (type-A). The type-A/B classification is determined by a single question: does the decoder structurally compose outputs from independently generated parts, or does it allow cross-segment information flow?

Type-A decoders (non-functorial). The transformer (WC) augments a standard transformer with a hard winding constraint: angle increments sum to the correct winding number by construction, but attention still mixes information across segments.11 1 An unconstrained transformer achieves 0%0\% winding accuracy and is excluded from all experiments. The cover decoder assigns a single independent network to each homotopy class—it respects winding but has no compositional structure, since each class is generated from scratch rather than assembled from parts; it is type-A not because of cross-segment information flow, but because it lacks monoidal factorization entirely. The transport attention decoder is designed to isolate the effect of the composition method: our framework derives its positional encoding (Appendix G), it has 3.4×3.4\times more parameters than the transport decoder, and it shares the winding constraint—yet it is type-A because attention still mixes across segments. If this decoder degrades on longer words, the cause is the composition method, not the conditioning.

Type-B decoders (functorial). The transport decoder is the Construction 3.2(i–ii) compilation: independent generator networks whose outputs are structurally concatenated. The homotopy decoder adds the learned 2-cell HH from Construction 3.2(iii), which witnesses group relations as continuous deformations between loops.

All architectures are trained with the same protocol: Chamfer loss optimized by AdamW (lr=10−3\mathrm{lr}=10^{-3}, weight decay 10−410^{-4}), cosine learning rate schedule, 500 epochs max with early stopping (patience 80). On T2T^{2}, all architectures converge to comparable training loss (2.232.23–2.272.27); on S1∨S1S^{1}\vee S^{1}, training losses differ (a matched-loss ablation in Appendix C confirms the gap is architectural, not statistical). Results are aggregated over 3 random seeds (mean ±\pm std). Full hyperparameters are in Appendix B.

Metrics.

The Chamfer distance dC​(P,Q)\mathrm{d_{C}}(P,Q) is the symmetric average nearest-neighbor squared distance between two point clouds—a standard metric in geometric deep learning, insensitive to parameterization (formula in Appendix B).

Definition 5.1 (Per-segment Chamfer distance).

Given a generated loop γ^\hat{\gamma} and ground-truth γ\gamma for a word ww of length LL, both loops are divided into LL segments (one per generator), each resampled to a fixed resolution of npts=32n_{\mathrm{pts}}=32 points. The per-segment Chamfer distance is:

d¯L​(w)=1L​∑i=1LdC​(γ^i,γi)\bar{d}_{L}(w)=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=1}^{L}\mathrm{d_{C}}(\hat{\gamma}_{i},\;\gamma_{i})

For a functorial decoder, d¯L=εgen\bar{d}_{L}=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{gen}} (constant) independent of LL. This is the primary metric in all experiments.

Circle accuracy (for S1∨S1S^{1}\vee S^{1} only): the fraction of generated segments whose centroid is closer to the correct circle (AA or BB) than to the wrong one. This detects a failure mode specific to non-abelian structure: a decoder that cannot distinguish which generator to trace will scatter segments across both circles.

5.1 Experiment 1: Torus T2T^{2} (π1=ℤ2\pi_{1}=\mathbb{Z}^{2}, abelian)

T2T^{2} is embedded in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} with major radius R=2.0R=2.0, minor radius r=0.8r=0.8. The generators a,ba,b trace loops around the two cycles.

At L=10L=10, the type-B range is 0.770.77–0.800.80 and the type-A range is 1.541.54–2.092.09: a 22–2.7×2.7\times gap. The transport attention decoder is especially informative: it shares the winding constraint, uses theoretically-motivated positional encoding, and has 3.4×3.4\times more parameters (585585K vs. 170170K)—yet degrades because cross-segment attention breaks functoriality. Correct conditioning cannot substitute for correct composition.

Two further observations sharpen the interpretation. First, the cover decoder has hard winding and factors through ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}, yet stagnates (2.15→1.912.15\to 1.91)—correct homotopy class is necessary but not sufficient; composition structure is required. Second, all architectures converge to comparable training loss (2.232.23–2.272.27; Appendix B), so the gap is not a training artifact.

On this abelian space, transport ≈\approx homotopy: the proof term is unnecessary because ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} has no non-trivial relations. The non-abelian experiments below remove the letter-counting crutch.

5.2 Experiment 2: S1∨S1S^{1}\vee S^{1} (π1=F2\pi_{1}=F_{2}, non-abelian free)

The theory makes a sharp prediction: the type-A/B gap should widen dramatically. On T2T^{2}, letter-counting partially compensated for the lack of functoriality; on S1∨S1S^{1}\vee S^{1}, the non-abelian fundamental group F2F_{2} removes this crutch. The decoder must now produce different loops for different orderings of the same letters—a​b≠b​aab\neq ba in F2F_{2}, and an architecture that collapses word order will fail categorically, not just quantitatively.

Setup.

S1∨S1S^{1}\vee S^{1} is embedded in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} as two unit circles meeting at the origin: circle AA in the x​yxy-plane centered at (−1,0,0)(-1,0,0), circle BB in the y​zyz-plane centered at (0,0,−1)(0,0,-1). A word w=w1⋯wLw=w_{1}\cdots w_{L} traces the loop that follows circle w1w_{1}, returns to the wedge point, follows circle w2w_{2}, and so on. A sequential decoder (GRU: a gated recurrent network that processes the word left-to-right, maintaining a hidden state) is included as a type-A baseline that respects sequential order.

The non-abelian separation.

The gap widens to 5.55.5–10×10\times: transport achieves 0.0540.054 at L=10L=10 while the transformer reaches 0.5370.537 (10×10\times) and the sequential decoder 0.2970.297 (5.5×5.5\times).

Topological collapse. Circle accuracy is the sharpest diagnostic. Even at L=2L=2 (a training length), the transformer assigns only 33%33\% of segments to the correct circle; by L=10L=10 this drops to 14%14\%—it cannot even distinguish which generator to trace, producing points near an arbitrary mixture of the two circles. This is a categorically different failure from T2T^{2}, where type-A decoders at least produced loops on the torus (with wrong per-segment geometry but correct topology). On S1∨S1S^{1}\vee S^{1}, the transformer collapses the non-abelian structure entirely, producing outputs that are topologically meaningless. The transport decoder maintains 100%100\% circle accuracy at all lengths.

The sequential decoder. The GRU outperforms the transformer at all lengths (0.2970.297 vs. 0.5370.537 at L=10L=10), consistent with the depth trichotomy (Appendix H): sequential processing helps with the prefix products that fixed-depth attention cannot compute. However, the GRU is still type-A—its segment generation depends on accumulated context, not structural composition—and it still degrades: per-segment Chamfer increases from 0.0100.010 to 0.2970.297 (30×30\times). Sequential processing is necessary but not sufficient for compositional generalization in non-abelian groups.

A matched-loss ablation (Appendix C) rules out training quality as the explanation: retraining type-A architectures with double epochs to match the best type-B training loss barely changes extrapolation (transformer d¯10\bar{d}_{10}: 0.537→0.4910.537\to 0.491, still 9×9\times worse; sequential: 0.297→0.2820.297\to 0.282, still 5×5\times worse). The gap is architectural, not statistical.

5.3 Experiment 3: Klein bottle KK (π1=ℤ⋊ℤ\pi_{1}=\mathbb{Z}\rtimes\mathbb{Z}) — the 2-cell

The first two experiments test Levels 0 and 1 of the hierarchy: winding constraints and monoidal composition. The Klein bottle tests Level 2: the learned proof term HH. The relation b​a​b−1=a−1bab^{-1}=a^{-1} means that traversing the bb-generator flips the orientation of aa: after going around bb, the aa-direction reverses. The theory predicts that HH should matter only for words that exercise this relation, and should be dormant otherwise.

The group ℤ⋊ℤ\mathbb{Z}\rtimes\mathbb{Z} is solvable, so the depth obstruction of §4 does not apply: constant-depth transformers have sufficient computational power for this group in principle [21]. The transformer’s failure on KK is therefore entirely due to the functoriality obstruction (Theorem 4.1), making KK a cleaner test of functoriality than S1∨S1S^{1}\vee S^{1}.

KK is embedded in ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4} via the standard half-angle twist parameterization. We test on two classes of words: Canonical words have all aa-generators before all bb-generators (e.g., a​a​b​baabb): the relation is not exercised, so the frame never flips mid-word. Non-canonical words interleave aa and bb (e.g., a​b​a​babab, b​a​abaa): the relation is exercised, requiring the decoder to track the flip.

The three decoders respond differently. The cover decoder factors through the abelianization ℤ⋊ℤ→ℤ2\mathbb{Z}\rtimes\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}^{2}, which collapses the relation entirely—it cannot distinguish b​aba from a​bab even though these represent different homotopy classes on KK. The transport decoder concatenates generators in word order and respects this distinction, but ignores the frame flip after bb. Only the homotopy decoder, with its learned proof term HH witnessing the relation, tracks the frame correctly.

Three results. (1) The proof term closes a 46% gap. On non-canonical words, homotopy achieves 0.820.82 vs. transport’s 1.521.52—a 1.85×1.85\times improvement entirely attributable to the learned 2-morphism HH. (2) On canonical words, transport ≈\approx homotopy (0.840.84 vs. 0.820.82): when the relation is not exercised, HH is dormant and adds no benefit. This confirms that the improvement is specifically due to the relation, not to additional capacity. (3) Homotopy eliminates the canonical/non-canonical asymmetry: transport’s non-canonical/canonical ratio is 1.8×1.8\times; homotopy’s is 1.0×1.0\times.

5.4 Cross-experiment summary

Each experiment validates a different level of the functorial hierarchy. T2T^{2}: winding constraints and monoidal composition (22–2.7×2.7\times gap). S1∨S1S^{1}\vee S^{1}: non-abelian amplification—attention is especially harmful when segment identity (which circle) must be preserved. KK: the learned 2-cell (natural transformation). Only the full HIT compilation—functorial composition plus proof terms—achieves uniformly low error across all spaces and word orderings.

6 Formalization and Verified Machine Learning

The experiments confirm that functorial architectures outperform non-functorial ones—but the theoretical guarantees are stronger than any finite experiment can demonstrate, because they hold for all parameter values and all word lengths. To make this claim precise, we formalize the core results in a proof assistant.

This inverts the standard approach to neural network verification. Post-hoc verification [13] attempts to prove properties of a trained network—computationally intractable for all but the simplest properties. Our approach verifies at design time: given a property PP (expressed as a homotopy type), construct an architecture that satisfies PP by construction, for all parameter values. Training adjusts geometric detail within the topologically correct constraint space; it cannot violate the type-theoretic guarantees.

The core positive and negative results are formalized in Cubical Agda (v2.6.4, --cubical --safe, no postulates) in four modules. Torus.agda: T2T^{2} as a HIT; transport commutativity (tra∘trb=trb∘tra\mathrm{tr}_{a}\circ\mathrm{tr}_{b}=\mathrm{tr}_{b}\circ\mathrm{tr}_{a}) holds definitionally. WedgeOfCircles.agda: a​b≠b​aab\neq ba in F2F_{2} (proved by case analysis on head letters). TransportCoherence.agda: Theorem 3.3—the transport decoder preserves monoidal structure—proved by induction on the first word, using associativity of concatenation. NonCompositionality.agda: the abstract schema of Theorem 4.1—transport coherence and global mixing are contradictory—proved as an impossibility theorem over any output type. The instantiation to softmax (that αi​j>0\alpha_{ij}>0 for all i,ji,j makes attention globally mixing) relies on the standard positivity of softmax, which is not formalized. The Klein bottle relation and proof term HH are not yet formalized; this would require extending the word type with inverses and formalizing the boundary conditions of the homotopy.

The guarantees form a hierarchy mirroring the Postnikov tower of the target space:

Level Guarantee Mechanism Validated by
0 Correct π1\pi_{1} class Hard winding constraint All 3 spaces
1 Monoidal composition Generator concatenation T2T^{2}, S1∨S1S^{1}\vee S^{1}
2 Group relations Learned proof term HH Klein bottle KK
≥3\geq 3 π2,π3,…\pi_{2},\pi_{3},\ldots Higher-dim. cells Future work

Each level adds architectural constraints that narrow the output space while preserving within-class expressivity (Appendix J). The three experiments validate levels 0–2; extending to higher homotopy groups remains open.

The result is a verified ML pipeline: specify (write a HIT), verify (prove properties in Cubical Agda), compile (apply Construction 3.2), train (standard gradient descent). The guarantees hold for the trained network at any parameter value, because they are properties of the architecture, not of the learned weights. To our knowledge, this is the first instance where machine-verified proofs provide compositional generalization guarantees for a neural architecture.

The long-term vision is a compiler from HIT specifications to certified neural architectures: parse a HIT declaration in Cubical Agda to extract generators, paths, and higher cells; assign each constructor to an architectural component per Construction 3.2; generate the hard constraints (winding, boundary conditions) as differentiable layers; and output a training script. This would make type-theoretic guarantees accessible to practitioners who specify their domain’s topology without requiring knowledge of HoTT.

7 Related Work

The framework draws on three lines of prior work: categorical foundations for deep learning, equivariant network design, and the empirical study of compositional generalization failures.

Categorical deep learning.

Cruttwell et al. [6] formalize gradient-based learning via lenses, parametric maps, and reverse derivative categories. Gavranović et al. [7] propose monads in a 2-category of parametric maps as a unified theory of architectures, recovering geometric deep learning constraints. Fong, Spivak, and Tuyéras [8] showed backpropagation is a functor; Spivak’s broader programme on compositionality [14] grounds the philosophical claim that systems compose functorially. We extend this lineage by constructing (not merely analyzing) functorial architectures from type-theoretic specifications.

Equivariant networks.

Cohen and Welling [15] and Weiler and Cesa [16] enforce f⁡(g⋅x)=g⋅f⁡(x)f(g\cdot x)=g\cdot f(x)—a constraint on a single morphism. Our functoriality is a constraint on the entire decoder: 𝒟⁡(g1⋅g2)=𝒟⁡(g1)⊕𝒟⁡(g2)\mathcal{D}(g_{1}\cdot g_{2})=\mathcal{D}(g_{1})\oplus\mathcal{D}(g_{2}). The distinction is not merely formal: the transport attention decoder (§5.1) has equivariant positional encoding derived from group theory, shares the winding constraint, and has 3.4×3.4\times more parameters than the transport decoder—yet degrades on longer words because cross-segment attention breaks functoriality. Equivariant conditioning (a morphism-level property) does not imply compositional generalization (a functor-level property).

Compositional generalization in ML.

Lake and Baroni [1], Kim and Linzen [2], and Dziri et al. [3] document systematic failures. Kobayashi et al. [17] find that an architectural bottleneck enables compositionality—our type-A/B distinction provides the categorical explanation: the bottleneck enforces monoidal factorization, i.e., functoriality.

Transformer expressivity and group composition.

Liu et al. [21] characterize the depth at which transformers can simulate finite-state automata, showing that solvable automata admit O⁡(1)O(1)-depth shortcuts (via Krohn-Rhodes decomposition) while nonsolvable automata require Ω⁡(log⁡T)\Omega(\log T) depth (via Barrington’s theorem). Their results yield the solvable/nonsolvable trichotomy in Corollary H.2 and make the Klein bottle (ℤ⋊ℤ\mathbb{Z}\rtimes\mathbb{Z}, solvable) a clean test of functoriality rather than depth. Concurrent work by Marchetti et al. [20] studies the same problem from the perspective of learning dynamics, proving width and depth separations for finite group composition. Their analysis is complementary: they characterize how networks learn group composition; we characterize which architectures preserve it and compile them from type-theoretic specifications.

We do not compare against methods developed for SCAN, COGS, or CFQ because the task types are incommensurable: discrete sequence transduction vs. continuous geometric generation, with exact-match accuracy vs. Chamfer distance. Running a SCAN-specialized architecture on loop generation, or our transport decoder on command parsing, would be a category error. However, the theoretical connection is direct: Theorem 4.1 (and its stronger form, Appendix F) applies to SCAN—the failure to generalize from a primitive command (“jump” seen in isolation) to its composed forms (“jump twice”, “jump around left”, etc.) is an instance of cross-segment dependencies corrupting compositional structure.

8 Conclusion

Compositional generalization is functoriality. HIT specifications provide a systematic source of functorial architectures: the compilation functor maps type-theoretic constructors to architectural components, guaranteeing monoidal preservation. Three experiments validate the full hierarchy—winding constraints, monoidal composition, and 2-cells witnessing group relations—with the Klein bottle experiment demonstrating the first neural architecture where a natural transformation is both theoretically necessary and empirically measurable.

The design principle is immediately actionable: when a task has compositional structure, use structural composition; attention-based architectures cannot learn this structure. This shifts the question from “can the network learn to compose?” to “does the architecture guarantee functoriality?” The plane with kk obstacles has π1=Fk\pi_{1}=F_{k}—our S1∨S1S^{1}\vee S^{1} experiment (π1=F2\pi_{1}=F_{2}) tests the same algebraic structure as 2-obstacle path planning, and the 5.55.5–10×10\times gap quantifies the advantage. Any domain with compositional structure—modular programs, multi-step plans, molecular ring systems—can be specified as a HIT and compiled into a certified architecture via the specify–verify–compile–train pipeline.

Limitations.

The framework currently handles π1\pi_{1} constraints. Extending to higher homotopy groups (π2\pi_{2}, π3\pi_{3}) would require higher-dimensional proof terms. The experiments use three spaces with relatively simple π1\pi_{1}; surfaces of higher genus would test HH more strenuously. For natural language, the theoretical results provide explanatory value, but the constructive approach awaits an appropriate formalization of linguistic compositional structure.

Code and data availability.

Cubical Agda formalization and Python code to replicate all experiments are available at https://github.com/karsar/hott_neuro.

Appendix A Full Proof of Theorem 4.1

The main text gives a proof sketch. Here we make the argument fully explicit, tracking the information flow through each attention layer to show exactly where functoriality breaks.

Proof.

Let TθT_{\theta} be a transformer with parameters θ\theta, LL layers of multi-head softmax self-attention, and embedding dimension dd. The input is a word w=w1⋯wnw=w_{1}\cdots w_{n} over generators of a non-trivial group GG, with each wiw_{i} embedded as hi(0)∈ℝdh_{i}^{(0)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Suppose for contradiction that TθT_{\theta} defines a monoidal functor: there exists ⊕\oplus such that Tθ​(w1⋅w2)=Tθ​(w1)⊕Tθ​(w2)T_{\theta}(w_{1}\cdot w_{2})=T_{\theta}(w_{1})\oplus T_{\theta}(w_{2}) for all w1,w2w_{1},w_{2}.

At layer ll, position ii in the w1w_{1}-segment computes: hi(l)=hi(l−1)+MHA(l)​(hi(l−1),{hj(l−1)}j)h_{i}^{(l)}=h_{i}^{(l-1)}+\mathrm{MHA}^{(l)}(h_{i}^{(l-1)},\{h_{j}^{(l-1)}\}_{j}), where multi-head attention aggregates: Attni=∑jαi​j​V​hj(l−1)\mathrm{Attn}_{i}=\sum_{j}\alpha_{ij}Vh_{j}^{(l-1)} with αi​j=softmaxj​(Q​hi(l−1)⋅K​hj(l−1)/d)\alpha_{ij}=\mathrm{softmax}_{j}(Qh_{i}^{(l-1)}\cdot Kh_{j}^{(l-1)}/\sqrt{d}).

For jj in the w2w_{2}-segment, the key K​hj(l−1)Kh_{j}^{(l-1)} depends on the embedding of w2w_{2}’s tokens. Since GG is non-trivial, there exist distinct words w2≠w2′w_{2}\neq w_{2}^{\prime} with [w2]=[w2′]∈G[w_{2}]=[w_{2}^{\prime}]\in G. These have different tokens, hence different embeddings, hence different keys, hence different αi​j\alpha_{ij}, hence different hi(1)h_{i}^{(1)} for i∈w1i\in w_{1}. Propagating through layers: Tθ​(w1⋅w2)≠Tθ​(w1⋅w2′)T_{\theta}(w_{1}\cdot w_{2})\neq T_{\theta}(w_{1}\cdot w_{2}^{\prime}).

But functoriality and Tθ​(w2)=Tθ​(w2′)T_{\theta}(w_{2})=T_{\theta}(w_{2}^{\prime}) require Tθ​(w1⋅w2)=Tθ​(w1)⊕Tθ​(w2)=Tθ​(w1)⊕Tθ​(w2′)=Tθ​(w1⋅w2′)T_{\theta}(w_{1}\cdot w_{2})=T_{\theta}(w_{1})\oplus T_{\theta}(w_{2})=T_{\theta}(w_{1})\oplus T_{\theta}(w_{2}^{\prime})=T_{\theta}(w_{1}\cdot w_{2}^{\prime}). Contradiction. ∎

Appendix B Training Details

Data generation.

For each training word, 1000 ground-truth loops are generated by tracing the standard geometric generators on XX with random phase offsets (uniformly distributed starting points along each generator circle) and small Gaussian noise (σ=0.02\sigma=0.02) applied independently to each output coordinate. This provides within-class geometric variation so that the network learns the shape of each homotopy class rather than memorizing a single curve.

Chamfer distance.

The Chamfer distance between two point clouds P={pi}i=1NP=\{p_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} and Q={qj}j=1MQ=\{q_{j}\}_{j=1}^{M} is:

dC​(P,Q)=12​N​∑iminj⁡‖pi−qj‖2+12​M​∑jmini⁡‖pi−qj‖2\mathrm{d_{C}}(P,Q)=\tfrac{1}{2N}\textstyle\sum_{i}\min_{j}\|p_{i}{-}q_{j}\|^{2}+\tfrac{1}{2M}\textstyle\sum_{j}\min_{i}\|p_{i}{-}q_{j}\|^{2}

Common protocol.

All experiments: Chamfer loss, AdamW optimizer (lr=10−3\mathrm{lr}=10^{-3}, weight decay 10−410^{-4}), cosine learning rate schedule with 20-epoch warmup, up to 500 epochs, early stopping (patience 80). Generator networks are 2-layer MLPs with 128 hidden units producing npts=32n_{\mathrm{pts}}=32 points per segment. All decoders output 64 points total, which for type-B decoders means L⋅32L\cdot 32 intermediate points resampled to 64. Seeds: 42, 179, 316.

T2T^{2}.

Embedded in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}. Training: 6 words ({a,b,a​a,a​b,b​a,b​b}\{a,b,aa,ab,ba,bb\}), 1000 samples each. Training losses: all architectures converge to 2.232.23–2.272.27. The homotopy decoder adds smoothness regularization (λ=0.05\lambda=0.05) on the proof term.

S1∨S1S^{1}\vee S^{1}.

Two unit circles in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} meeting at origin. Same 6 training words (but a​b≠b​aab\neq ba). Training losses: transport 0.0023±0.00030.0023\pm 0.0003, transformer 0.0030±0.00020.0030\pm 0.0002, sequential 0.0051±0.00020.0051\pm 0.0002.

Klein bottle KK.

Embedded in ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4} via half-angle twist. Training: all 16 words of length ≤2\leq 2 in {a,a−1,b,b−1}\{a,a^{-1},b,b^{-1}\}. The proof term HH is a 2-layer MLP (64 hidden units) with boundaries H⁡(s=0)=gb⊕gaH(s{=}0)=g_{b}\oplus g_{a}, H⁡(s=1)=ga−1⊕gbH(s{=}1)=g_{a^{-1}}\oplus g_{b}, trained jointly with generators. Training losses: cover 0.8310.831, transport 0.9200.920, homotopy 0.9200.920, transformer WC 0.8510.851 (all ±<0.02\pm{<}0.02).

Appendix C Matched-Loss Ablation

A natural objection to the main results is that type-A architectures simply need more training. We test this directly: if we retrain type-A decoders to match the type-B training loss, does the extrapolation gap close?

To rule out training quality as the explanation for the type-A/B gap, we retrained type-A architectures on S1∨S1S^{1}\vee S^{1} with 2×2\times epochs and reduced learning rate (5×10−45\times 10^{-4}), targeting the best type-B training loss.

Train loss d¯10\bar{d}_{10}
Architecture Original Retrained Original Retrained
Transformer .0030.0030 .0030.0030 .537.537 .491.491
Sequential .0051.0051 .0054.0054 .297.297 .282.282
Transport (ref.) .0023.0023 .054.054

Neither type-A architecture can reach the type-B training loss even with 2×2\times epochs: the transformer stays at 0.00300.0030 (target 0.00230.0023), the sequential worsens to 0.00540.0054 (from 0.00510.0051 with standard training; the lower learning rate finds a different basin). This is itself an architectural limitation: the compositional structure of the transport decoder helps optimization, not just generalization. The per-segment Chamfer at L=10L=10 barely changes after retraining: transformer .537→.491.537\to.491 (still 9×9\times worse than transport), sequential .297→.282.297\to.282 (still 5×5\times worse). The gap is architectural.

The main text reports selected lengths to save space. The full trajectories below reveal how degradation unfolds: whether it is gradual or abrupt, and whether it saturates.

The transformer’s 33%33\% at L=2L=2 (a training length) shows that the failure is not merely extrapolation—it cannot represent non-abelian structure even in-distribution. The sequential decoder starts better (67%67\%) but converges to the same floor.

The S1∨S1S^{1}\vee S^{1} tables reveal the degradation trajectory: the transformer is already at 33%33\% circle accuracy at L=2L=2 (a training length), confirming that the failure is fundamental, not merely an extrapolation issue. Appendix E Coherence Battery

Per-segment Chamfer measures how well each segment is generated. But functoriality also implies structural identities—exact zeros, not approximate ones. The following battery tests whether these identities hold, distinguishing architectural guarantees from learned approximations.

For T2T^{2}, we test four structural coherence properties. Composition gap: d∞​(𝒟⁡(w1)⊕𝒟⁡(w2),𝒟⁡(w1​w2))d_{\infty}(\mathcal{D}(w_{1})\oplus\mathcal{D}(w_{2}),\;\mathcal{D}(w_{1}w_{2})) for canonical pairs. Commutativity: d∞​(𝒟⁡(a​b),𝒟⁡(b​a))d_{\infty}(\mathcal{D}(ab),\mathcal{D}(ba)). Reordering gap: d∞​(𝒟⁡(b)⊕𝒟⁡(a),𝒟⁡(a​b))d_{\infty}(\mathcal{D}(b)\oplus\mathcal{D}(a),\;\mathcal{D}(ab)). Non-canonical: d∞​(𝒟⁡(abab),𝒟⁡(aabb))d_{\infty}(\mathcal{D}(\texttt{abab}),\mathcal{D}(\texttt{aabb})).

Commutativity and non-canonical gaps are exactly zero for cover, transport, and homotopy (they factor through ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}, so a​bab and b​aba produce identical output by construction). Transport attention shows 1.54±1.391.54\pm 1.39: learned coherence is fragile and high-variance, while structural coherence is exact.

Order sensitivity on S1∨S1S^{1}\vee S^{1}.

We test whether each decoder distinguishes words that differ only in generator order (e.g., a​bab vs. b​aba, a​a​baab vs. a​b​aaba)—all distinct homotopy classes in F2F_{2}. Transport distinguishes 80%80\% of test pairs (the remaining 20%20\% have cross-Chamfer near the noise floor, reflecting geometric similarity rather than architectural failure). The transformer distinguishes only 40±16%40\pm 16\%—barely above chance—confirming that attention collapses word order.

Appendix F General Non-Compositionality of Attention

Theorem 4.1 in the main text uses group structure. A natural question is whether groups are essential to the argument, or whether the obstruction is more fundamental. The following result shows it is the latter: softmax attention is incompatible with any form of sequential compositionality, regardless of algebraic structure.

Definition F.1 (Segment-independent compositionality).

A decoder 𝒟:Σ∗→𝒴\mathcal{D}:\Sigma^{*}\to\mathcal{Y} is segment-independently compositional if there exists a combination operation ⊕\oplus on 𝒴\mathcal{Y} such that:

  1. (i)

    𝒟⁡(w1⋅w2)=𝒟⁡(w1)⊕𝒟⁡(w2)\mathcal{D}(w_{1}\cdot w_{2})=\mathcal{D}(w_{1})\oplus\mathcal{D}(w_{2}) for all words w1,w2w_{1},w_{2};

  2. (ii)

    𝒟⁡(w)\mathcal{D}(w) is computed from ww alone;

  3. (iii)

    ⊕\oplus does not introduce cross-segment interactions: when 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is a sequence, the output positions corresponding to w1w_{1} are determined by 𝒟⁡(w1)\mathcal{D}(w_{1}) alone.

Theorem F.2 (General non-compositionality of attention).

Let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be a network containing at least one softmax attention layer over the full input sequence. Then 𝒯\mathcal{T} is not segment-independently compositional for any alphabet |Σ|≥2|\Sigma|\geq 2, for generic parameters (Q,K,V)(Q,K,V).

Proof.

We show condition (iii) is violated. At the first attention layer applied to w1⋅w2w_{1}\cdot w_{2}, position ii within the w1w_{1} segment computes: hi′=∑j∈w1αi​j​V​hj+∑j∈w2αi​j​V​hjh_{i}^{\prime}=\sum_{j\in w_{1}}\alpha_{ij}Vh_{j}+\sum_{j\in w_{2}}\alpha_{ij}Vh_{j}, where αi​j=softmax⁡(Q​hi⋅K​hj/d)\alpha_{ij}=\mathrm{softmax}(Qh_{i}\cdot Kh_{j}/\sqrt{d}). The cross-segment sum depends on the tokens of w2w_{2} through both αi​j\alpha_{ij} and V​hjVh_{j}. For generic (Q,K,V)(Q,K,V) and |Σ|≥2|\Sigma|\geq 2, replacing any token in w2w_{2} changes K​hjKh_{j} and V​hjVh_{j}, hence changes hi′h_{i}^{\prime}. Therefore the output at position i∈w1i\in w_{1} depends on the content of w2w_{2}, violating condition (iii). ∎

Remark F.3.

This theorem requires no group structure, no topology, and no specific target space. It provides a structural explanation for why transformers struggle with compositional generalization across SCAN, COGS, and CFQ—the obstacle is architectural, not task-specific. The result fails for causal attention with a hard segment partition (where positions in w1w_{1} attend only to w1w_{1}), but such masking prevents w1w_{1}’s representation from depending on w2w_{2}—precisely the loss of global context that motivates full attention.

Corollary F.4 (Structural limits on learned compositionality).

Theorems 4.1 and F.2 do not imply that a transformer cannot learn to approximate compositional behaviour on the training distribution. What they constrain is the nature of any such learned compositionality:

  1. (a)

    Approximate, never exact. The cross-segment attention term ∑j∈w2αi​j​V​hj\sum_{j\in w_{2}}\alpha_{ij}Vh_{j} is architecturally present and strictly positive (softmax>0\mathrm{softmax}>0). Training can make this term small but not zero.

  2. (b)

    Distribution-dependent. The suppression of cross-segment attention is learned for the specific input statistics (word lengths, winding ranges, token frequencies) encountered during training.

  3. (c)

    No length transfer guarantee. For L>LtrainL>L_{\mathrm{train}}, the cross-segment attention weights that were learned-to-be-small on training data have no architectural reason to remain small. The quality of learned compositionality may degrade smoothly, abruptly, or not at all—this is an empirical question, not a structural guarantee.

Proof.

(a) By the strict positivity of softmax, αi​j>0\alpha_{ij}>0 for all (i,j)(i,j), so the cross-segment sum is nonzero whenever V​hj≠0Vh_{j}\neq 0 (which holds generically). (b) The trained parameters (Q,K,V)(Q,K,V) minimize a loss on the training distribution; there is no penalty on cross-segment attention magnitude as such. (c) At length L>LtrainL>L_{\mathrm{train}}, both the number of cross-segment terms and the positional encodings (at untrained positions) change; the learned suppression was not trained for these configurations. ∎

Appendix G Abelian Transport-Attention Theorem

The transport attention decoder in our experiments uses a positional encoding derived from the framework rather than chosen ad hoc. This appendix shows that the derivation recovers a well-known technique—rotary position embeddings (RoPE)—as a special case, and explains why principled positions alone are insufficient for compositional generalization.

The main text notes that the framework derives 2D rotary positional encoding from group theory. Here we state the full result.

Definition G.1 (Transport-structured attention).

Let GG be a finitely generated abelian group with generators g1,…,gkg_{1},\ldots,g_{k}. For each generator gig_{i}, let Ti∈O⁡(d)T_{i}\in O(d) be a learnable orthogonal matrix. The transport-structured attention at position pp with group element γp∈G\gamma_{p}\in G is:

αp​q=softmax(qp⋅Tγq−γp​kqd),Tγ=T1n1⋯Tknk for γ=(n1,…,nk).\alpha_{pq}=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{q_{p}\cdot T_{\gamma_{q}-\gamma_{p}}\,k_{q}}{\sqrt{d}}\right),\qquad T_{\gamma}=T_{1}^{n_{1}}\cdots T_{k}^{n_{k}}\text{ for }\gamma=(n_{1},\ldots,n_{k}). (1)
Theorem G.2 (Abelian transport attention).

Let GG be a finitely generated abelian group. Then:

  1. (a)

    Transport-structured attention (1) is well-defined: TγT_{\gamma} is independent of the decomposition of γ\gamma into generators (since GG is abelian and the TiT_{i} commute as orthogonal matrices with matching rotation planes).

  2. (b)

    The computational cost is O⁡(T2​d)O(T^{2}d)—identical to standard attention.

  3. (c)

    When TiT_{i} acts as block-diagonal rotations on d/2d/2 independent planes, this reduces to 2​k2k-dimensional rotary position embeddings (RoPE) [18]. Standard RoPE is the G=ℤG=\mathbb{Z} special case; the framework gives the natural G=ℤkG=\mathbb{Z}^{k} extension.

Proof.

(a) For abelian GG, each γ\gamma has a unique decomposition γ=n1​g1+⋯+nk​gk\gamma=n_{1}g_{1}+\cdots+n_{k}g_{k}. Block-diagonal rotations on the same planes commute (angles add), so Tγ=T1n1⋯TknkT_{\gamma}=T_{1}^{n_{1}}\cdots T_{k}^{n_{k}} is independent of ordering. (b) Computing Tγq−γpT_{\gamma_{q}-\gamma_{p}} requires kk matrix powers in O⁡(d)O(d) each (block-diagonal); the dominant cost is T2T^{2} pairwise computations at O⁡(d)O(d) each. (c) With TiT_{i} block-diagonal having 2×22\times 2 rotation blocks R⁡(ωi​j)R(\omega_{ij}), the transport TinT_{i}^{n} acts as R⁡(n​ωi​j)R(n\omega_{ij}) on each plane. The combined TγT_{\gamma} acts as R⁡(∑ini​ωi​j)R(\sum_{i}n_{i}\omega_{ij})—exactly multi-dimensional RoPE with frequency vectors ωi=(ωi​1,…,ωi,d/2)\omega_{i}=(\omega_{i1},\ldots,\omega_{i,d/2}). ∎

Remark G.3.

This explains why RoPE improves length generalization: it implements transport in the universal cover of the classifying space of ℤ\mathbb{Z}. However, transport-structured positional encoding does not make the decoder type-B (functorial): the attention mechanism still mixes information across segments. The transport attention decoder in our experiments confirms this—it has principled positions but wrong composition, and degrades like any type-A architecture.

Appendix H Depth Obstruction and RNN–Transformer Trichotomy

Why does the sequential decoder (GRU) outperform the transformer on S1∨S1S^{1}\vee S^{1} but not match the transport decoder? The answer involves two independent obstructions. The first is functoriality: attention mixes across segments for any non-trivial group (Theorem 4.1). The second is depth: for groups with nonsolvable finite quotients, computing prefix products requires depth Ω⁡(log⁡n)\Omega(\log n), which fixed-depth transformers cannot provide. For solvable groups, however, constant-depth shortcuts exist [21], so the depth obstruction vanishes—only the functoriality obstruction remains. The GRU has the right depth (sequential scan) but the wrong composition (context-dependent, not structural), which is why it outperforms the transformer on F2F_{2} yet still falls far short of the transport decoder.

Theorem H.1 (Depth obstruction for prefix products).

Let GG be a finitely generated non-abelian group. Any transport-coherent attention mechanism for GG requires computing the accumulated group element γp=gw1⋅gw2⋯gwp\gamma_{p}=g_{w_{1}}\cdot g_{w_{2}}\cdots g_{w_{p}} for each prefix of the input. This prefix-product computation:

  1. (a)

    Cannot be performed by a fixed-depth transformer when GG surjects onto a nonsolvable finite group. A fixed-depth transformer implements a bounded-depth, unbounded-fan-in computation—the circuit class 𝖠𝖢0\mathsf{AC}^{0}. The free group F2F_{2} surjects onto nonsolvable finite groups (e.g., S5S_{5}, which is 22-generated), and the word problem for any nonsolvable finite group is 𝖭𝖢1\mathsf{NC}^{1}-complete under 𝖠𝖢0\mathsf{AC}^{0} reductions [12]. Since 𝖭𝖢1⊄𝖠𝖢0\mathsf{NC}^{1}\not\subset\mathsf{AC}^{0} (parity separates them), computing prefix products in F2F_{2} is at least as hard as solving these word problems, and hence outside 𝖠𝖢0\mathsf{AC}^{0}. For solvable groups, this obstruction does not apply: Liu et al. [21] show that all solvable semiautomata admit constant-depth Transformer simulators via the Krohn-Rhodes decomposition (their Theorem 2), though the resulting shortcuts are empirically brittle and do not generalize out of distribution.

  2. (b)

    Requires Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) total work (each prefix product depends on the full prefix, and non-commutativity prevents any shortcut).

  3. (c)

    Can be performed by an associative scan (parallel prefix) in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) depth with O⁡(n)O(n) work—a sequential-scan structure absent from standard transformers but present in state space models [19] and recurrent architectures. Marchetti et al. [20] prove this rigorously for finite groups: they construct explicit RNN solutions that compose in O⁡(k)O(k) steps and multilayer MLP solutions that compose in O⁡(log⁡k)O(\log k) layers, both with hidden width O⁡(|G|3/2)O(|G|^{3/2}) independent of sequence length—compared to the O⁡(exp⁡k)O(\exp k) width required by two-layer networks.

Proof.

(a) The key is the circuit-complexity classification of group word problems. Barrington [12] showed that the word problem for any fixed nonsolvable group GG—deciding whether a product of generators equals the identity—is complete for 𝖭𝖢1\mathsf{NC}^{1} (fan-in 22, depth O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n)) under 𝖠𝖢0\mathsf{AC}^{0} reductions (bounded-depth, unbounded-fan-in circuits). Since 𝖭𝖢1⊄𝖠𝖢0\mathsf{NC}^{1}\not\subset\mathsf{AC}^{0} (the parity function is in 𝖭𝖢1\mathsf{NC}^{1} but not in 𝖠𝖢0\mathsf{AC}^{0}), no 𝖠𝖢0\mathsf{AC}^{0} circuit can solve these word problems. The free group F2F_{2} surjects onto S5S_{5} (which is 22-generated and nonsolvable): the natural quotient map F2↠S5F_{2}\twoheadrightarrow S_{5} reduces the word problem for S5S_{5} to computing prefix products in F2F_{2}. A fixed-depth transformer with a fixed number of layers implements a bounded-depth, unbounded-fan-in computation—that is, an 𝖠𝖢0\mathsf{AC}^{0} circuit—and therefore cannot compute these products. The converse—solvable groups admit constant-depth solutions—follows from Liu et al. [21], who apply the Krohn-Rhodes decomposition to factor solvable semiautomata into modular counters and memory units, each simulable at depth 11. (b) The prefix product γp\gamma_{p} depends on all pp inputs; since GG is non-abelian, no proper subset determines γp\gamma_{p}. (c) Group multiplication is associative, so the parallel prefix algorithm computes all nn prefix products in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) depth with O⁡(n)O(n) multiplications. ∎

Corollary H.2 (Depth trichotomy).

The computational requirements for prefix products depend on the solvability structure of GG, yielding three regimes:

  1. (a)

    Abelian. The product depends only on letter counts, computable in 𝖠𝖢0\mathsf{AC}^{0}. Bounded-depth parallel attention suffices for the computation.

  2. (b)

    Solvable non-abelian (e.g. ℤ⋊ℤ\mathbb{Z}\rtimes\mathbb{Z}). Constant-depth shortcuts exist via Krohn-Rhodes decomposition [21], with depth independent of sequence length but potentially large width. Fixed-depth transformers have sufficient computational power for prefix products, but attention still mixes across segments, so the functoriality obstruction (Theorem 4.1) remains.

  3. (c)

    Nonsolvable quotients (e.g. F2↠S5F_{2}\twoheadrightarrow S_{5}). Prefix products are 𝖭𝖢1\mathsf{NC}^{1}-complete, outside 𝖠𝖢0\mathsf{AC}^{0}. Fixed-depth transformers fail for two independent reasons: insufficient depth and broken functoriality.

Functoriality (Theorem 4.1) is the uniform obstruction across all three cases. Depth is an additional obstruction only in case (c).

Proof.

(a) For abelian GG, the product g1⋯gng_{1}\cdots g_{n} depends only on the multiplicity of each generator, which is a sum—computable by 𝖠𝖢0\mathsf{AC}^{0} circuits. (b) Liu et al. [21] show that all solvable semiautomata admit O⁡(1)O(1)-depth Transformer simulators (their Theorem 2), via the Krohn-Rhodes decomposition into modular counters and memory units. Since every finite quotient of a solvable group is solvable, prefix products in any solvable GG can be computed at constant depth. However, constant-depth computability does not imply functoriality: by Theorem 4.1, the attention mechanism still mixes token-level information across segments. (c) Theorem H.1(a): Barrington’s theorem plus 𝖭𝖢1⊄𝖠𝖢0\mathsf{NC}^{1}\not\subset\mathsf{AC}^{0}. ∎

The GRU’s intermediate performance on S1∨S1S^{1}\vee S^{1} (0.2970.297 vs. transformer’s 0.5370.537, transport’s 0.0540.054) confirms case (c): the GRU has the right depth structure (sequential processing) but the wrong composition structure (context-dependent, not structural). On the Klein bottle, the transformer’s failure illustrates case (b): even when depth is not an obstruction, cross-segment attention prevents functorial composition.

Appendix I Per-Segment Error Scaling

The experiments show that type-B error is flat in LL while type-A error grows. Is this an accident of specific architectures, or does it follow from the theorems? Here we prove it follows: functoriality implies O⁡(1)O(1) scaling, while non-functoriality implies Ω⁡(1)\Omega(1) degradation for L≫LtrainL\gg L_{\mathrm{train}}.

Proposition I.1 (Per-segment error scaling).

Let d¯L=𝔼w:|w|=L[Chamfer(𝒟(w),𝒟∗(w))]/L\bar{d}_{L}=\mathbb{E}_{w:|w|=L}[\mathrm{Chamfer}(\mathcal{D}(w),\mathcal{D}^{*}(w))]/L denote the per-segment Chamfer distance for words of length LL.

  1. (a)

    Type-B: For a transport decoder with converged training, d¯L≤maxi⁡Chamfer⁡(gi​(θ),gi∗)+η⁡(L)/L→L→∞εgen\bar{d}_{L}\leq\max_{i}\mathrm{Chamfer}(g_{i}(\theta),g_{i}^{*})+\eta(L)/L\xrightarrow{L\to\infty}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{gen}}, where εgen\varepsilon_{\mathrm{gen}} is the generator approximation error, independent of LL.

  2. (b)

    Type-A: For type-A architectures tested at L>LtrainL>L_{\mathrm{train}}, d¯L≥Ω⁡(e⁡(L−Ltrain))\bar{d}_{L}\geq\Omega(e(L-L_{\mathrm{train}})) where e⁡(⋅)e(\cdot) is the extrapolation error of the network’s learned functions beyond their training domain. For the cover decoder, the MLP evaluates at winding magnitudes up to LL (trained only to LtrainL_{\mathrm{train}}), giving e=Ω⁡(L−Ltrain)e=\Omega(L-L_{\mathrm{train}}) by the Taylor remainder. For transport attention, 2D RoPE rotation angles scale as na/Ltrainn_{a}/L_{\mathrm{train}} times any training angle, placing attention in an untrained regime. For the transformer (WC), attention patterns at length LL involve L2L^{2} pairwise interactions vs. Ltrain2L_{\mathrm{train}}^{2} during training; the learned attention weights have no architectural reason to generalize to the longer-range interactions. In all cases, d¯L=Ω⁡(1)\bar{d}_{L}=\Omega(1) for L≫LtrainL\gg L_{\mathrm{train}}.

Proof.

(a) By Theorem 3.3, Chamfer⁡(𝒟⁡(w),𝒟∗​(w))≤L⋅εgen+η⁡(L)\mathrm{Chamfer}(\mathcal{D}(w),\mathcal{D}^{*}(w))\leq L\cdot\varepsilon_{\mathrm{gen}}+\eta(L), where η⁡(L)\eta(L) accounts for resampling (O⁡(L)O(\sqrt{L}) interpolation error). Dividing by LL: d¯L≤εgen+η⁡(L)/L→εgen\bar{d}_{L}\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{gen}}+\eta(L)/L\to\varepsilon_{\mathrm{gen}}.

(b) A word of length LL has winding pair (na,nb)(n_{a},n_{b}) with na+nb=Ln_{a}+n_{b}=L. The cover decoder’s MLP evaluates at ‖(na,nb)‖\|(n_{a},n_{b})\| up to LL, while training covered only ‖(na,nb)‖≤Ltrain\|(n_{a},n_{b})\|\leq L_{\mathrm{train}}. For smooth functions, extrapolation error is Ω⁡(‖x−xtrain‖)\Omega(\|x-x_{\mathrm{train}}\|). For transport attention, rotation angles are na/Ltrainn_{a}/L_{\mathrm{train}} times larger than any training angle. For the transformer (WC), the number of cross-segment attention pairs grows as (L−Ltrain)(L-L_{\mathrm{train}}) new positions per segment, each contributing untrained interactions. All three mechanisms give per-position error Ω⁡(L−Ltrain)\Omega(L-L_{\mathrm{train}}), hence d¯L=Ω⁡((L−Ltrain)/L)=Ω⁡(1)\bar{d}_{L}=\Omega((L-L_{\mathrm{train}})/L)=\Omega(1) for L≫LtrainL\gg L_{\mathrm{train}}. ∎

Appendix J Expressivity of Transport Decoders

A natural concern is that functoriality constrains the decoder so tightly that it cannot represent interesting loops. The following result shows this is not the case: within each homotopy class, the transport decoder is a universal approximator. The constraint acts only between classes, enforcing composition.

Proposition J.1 (Expressivity).

Let 𝒟θtr\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{tr}}_{\theta} be a transport decoder with generator networks ga​(θ),gb​(θ)g_{a}(\theta),g_{b}(\theta). Let ℒn⊂ℒ⁡(X)\mathcal{L}_{n}\subset\mathcal{L}(X) denote the space of loops with homotopy class n∈Gn\in G. Then:

  1. (a)

    Within-class expressivity: Each generator ga​(θ)g_{a}(\theta) can represent any continuous loop in ℒ(1,0)\mathcal{L}_{(1,0)} given sufficient network capacity (by the universal approximation theorem applied to the generator network in polar coordinates).

  2. (b)

    Between-class constraint: For homotopy class (na,nb)(n_{a},n_{b}), the output is the nan_{a}-fold concatenation of gag_{a} followed by nbn_{b}-fold concatenation of gbg_{b}. The geometric degrees of freedom are those of gag_{a} and gbg_{b} alone.

  3. (c)

    Degrees of freedom: The number of independent geometric degrees of freedom equals the number of generators in the group presentation.

The cover decoder has strictly more geometric freedom (an independent shape per homotopy class), but this extra freedom is precisely the freedom to be incoherent.

Proof.

(a) Universal approximation in polar coordinates. (b) By construction of the transport decoder. (c) For ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}, the group is free abelian on two generators; the transport decoder factors through canonical form ana​bnba^{n_{a}}b^{n_{b}}, making the two generator shapes the only free parameters. ∎

Appendix K Resampling Artifact Analysis

Comparing loops of different lengths with a fixed-resolution metric creates a subtle confound. This appendix shows that our per-segment Chamfer metric avoids it, and quantifies how large the artifact would be with a naive alternative.

All decoders produce a fixed-length output of Tout=64T_{\mathrm{out}}=64 points regardless of word length LL. This creates a systematic confound: as LL grows, the underlying curve lengthens while point density drops, causing naive Chamfer distance to decrease even when per-segment error is constant.

We verified this with synthetic curves under constant additive noise σ=0.1\sigma=0.1:

L=2L{=}2 L=4L{=}4 L=8L{=}8 L=10L{=}10
Per-seg Chamfer (fair, 32 pts/seg) 0.026 0.024 0.029 0.026
Per-seg Chamfer (naive, resample to 64) 0.010 0.003 0.002 0.001
Artifact ratio (naive/fair) 0.4×0.4\times 0.1×0.1\times 0.07×0.07\times 0.05×0.05\times

The fair metric (comparing each segment at fixed 32 points) is flat (∼0.026\sim 0.026), as expected for constant noise. The naive metric decreases by 10×10\times from L=2L{=}2 to L=10L{=}10—a pure measurement artifact. Our per-segment Chamfer d¯L\bar{d}_{L} in all experiments avoids this by comparing each of the LL segments at a fixed resolution of 32 points, ensuring that the metric measures generalization quality, not resampling fidelity.
